question: The corpus contains both the 2019 ratified RISC-V specification (version 20191213) and the 2025 Unprivileged ISA manual (version 20250508). Which should control an answer about the current definition of a base integer instruction such as JALR, and how may the 2019 edition still be used?

2.5. Control Transfer Instructions | Page 31

The indirect jump instruction JALR (jump and link register) uses the I-type encoding. The target
address is obtained by adding the sign-extended 12-bit I-immediate to the register rs1, then setting
the least-significant bit of the result to zero. The address of the instruction following the jump (pc+4) is
written to register rd. Register x0 can be used as the destination if the result is not required.

Plain unconditional indirect jumps (assembler pseudoinstruction JR) are encoded as a JALR with rd=

x0. Procedure returns in the standard calling convention (assembler pseudoinstruction RET) are
encoded as a JALR with rd=x0, rs1=x1, and imm=0.

The term call is used to refer to a JAL or JALR instruction with a link register as destination, i.e., rd≠x0.
Conventionally, the link register is x1 or x5. A call using JAL or C.JAL is termed a direct call. A C.JALR
expands to JALR x1, 0(rs1) and is a call. A call using JALR or C.JALR is termed an indirect-call.

The term return is used to refer to a JALR instruction with rd=x0 and with rs1=x1 or rs1=x5. A C.JR
instruction expands to JALR x0, 0(rs1) and is a return if rs1=x1 or rs1=x5.

The term indirect-jump is used to refer to a JALR instruction with rd=x0 and where the rs1 is not x1 or x5
(i.e., not a return). A C.JR instruction where rs1 is not x1 or x5 (i.e., not a return) is an indirect-jump.

The RVC standard extension for compressed instructions provides unconditional jump and conditional

results.title: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged ISA (document version 20191213)
results.text:
2.5  Control Transfer Instructions

RV32I provides two types of control transfer instructions: unconditional jumps and conditional
branches. Control transfer instructions in RV32I do not have architecturally visible delay slots.

Unconditional Jumps
The jump and link (JAL) instruction uses the J-type format, where the J-immediate encodes a

signed offset in multiples of 2 bytes. The offset is sign-extended and added to the address of the
jump instruction to form the jump target address. Jumps can therefore target a ±1 MiB range.
JAL stores the address of the instruction following the jump (pc+4) into register rd. The standard
software calling convention uses x1 as the return address register and x5 as an alternate link register.

results.title: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged ISA (document version 20191213)
results.text:
The unconditional jump instructions all use PC-relative addressing to help support position-independent code. The JALR instruction was defined to enable a two-instruction sequence to
    jump anywhere in a 32-bit absolute address range. A LUI instruction can first load rs1 with the
    upper 20 bits of a target address, then JALR can add in the lower bits. Similarly, AUIPC then
    JALR can jump anywhere in a 32-bit pc-relative address range.
      Note that the JALR instruction does not treat the 12-bit immediate as multiples of 2 bytes,
    unlike the conditional branch instructions. This avoids one more immediate format in hardware.
    In practice, most uses of JALR will have either a zero immediate or be paired with a LUI or
    AUIPC, so the slight reduction in range is not significant.

results.title: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged ISA (document version 20191213)
results.text:
Clearing the least-significant bit when calculating the JALR target address both simplifies
    the hardware slightly and allows the low bit of function pointers to be used to store auxiliary
    information. Although there is potentially a slight loss of error checking in this case, in practice
    jumps to an incorrect instruction address will usually quickly raise an exception.
      When used with a base rs1=x0, JALR can be used to implement a single instruction subroutine call to the lowest 2 KiB or highest 2 KiB address region from anywhere in the address space,
    which could be used to implement fast calls to a small runtime library. Alternatively, an ABI
    could dedicate a general-purpose register to point to a library elsewhere in the address space.
The JAL and JALR instructions will generate an instruction-address-misaligned exception if the
target address is not aligned to a four-byte boundary.

args.answer:
**Which edition controls:** For any question about the *current* definition of a base integer instruction such as JALR, the 2025 Unprivileged Architecture manual (document version 20250508) is authoritative and controls the answer; the 20191213 edition is the earlier ratified ISA and is used only for history or comparison, not as the current rule. The 2025 manual is the one that includes "all ratified extensions through February 2025" and that deliberately removed unratified content — for example the draft Zam extension (replaced by a misaligned atomicity granule PMA) and the sketch of the RV128I base ISA — so its text is the up-to-date statement of the architecture [2].

**What the controlling text says about JALR:** In the 2025 manual, "The indirect jump instruction JALR (jump and link register) uses the I-type encoding. The target address is obtained by adding the sign-extended 12-bit I-immediate to the register rs1, then setting the least-significant bit of the result to zero. The address of the instruction following the jump (pc+4) is written to register rd. Register x0 can be used as the destination if the result is not required." It also states that plain unconditional indirect jumps (pseudoinstruction JR) are a JALR with rd=x0, and that a standard-convention procedure return (pseudoinstruction RET) is a JALR with rd=x0, rs1=x1, and imm=0 [1].

**How the 2019 edition may still be used:**
1. *As a cross-check that the rule has not changed.* The 2019 manual gives the same JALR definition word for word — I-type encoding, sign-extended 12-bit I-immediate added to rs1 with the least-significant bit cleared, pc+4 written to rd, x0 usable as destination [3]. So for JALR itself, citing the 2025 text and noting the 2019 text agrees is a legitimate historical confirmation, not a competing rule.
2. *For design rationale and commentary that the current manual does not restate.* The 2019 edition explains why JALR was defined the way it was: it enables a two-instruction LUI+JALR (or AUIPC+JALR) sequence to reach a 32-bit absolute or pc-relative address range; unlike conditional branches, its 12-bit immediate is *not* treated as multiples of 2 bytes; and clearing the least-significant bit both simplifies hardware slightly and lets the low bit of function pointers store auxiliary information. It also notes JAL and JALR raise an instruction-address-misaligned exception if the target is not four-byte aligned [4][5].
3. *For historical/versioning context.* The 2019-era preface material preserved in the 2025 manual records how the base integer ISA was bumped to version 2.1 "reflecting the presence of the ratified RVWMO memory model and exclusion of FENCE.I, counters, and CSR instructions that were in previous base ISA," and how the document name changed to "unprivileged" as ISA specifications were separated from platform profile mandates [6]. Comparing module status tables across editions (e.g. which extensions were Draft/Frozen then versus Ratified now) is likewise a legitimate historical use.
4. *For wording of older text you are actually reading.* If a course text, assembler, or older document quotes the 2019 phrasing — e.g. its note that C.JALR "does not expand exactly to a base RVI instruction as the value added to the PC to form the link address is 2 rather than 4 as in the base ISA" — the 2019 manual is the right source for what that edition said [7].

**Where the editions actually differ in scope:** the 2025 manual carries material the 2019 edition cannot answer, such as the ratified Zicfiss/Zicfilp landing-pad and shadow-stack terminology built on call/return conventions — a call is a JAL or JALR with a link register (x1 or x5) as destination, a return is a JALR with rd=x0 and rs1=x1 or x5, and an indirect-jump is a JALR with rd=x0 whose rs1 is neither x1 nor x5 [8]. Bottom line: cite 20250508 for the rule; cite 20191213 only to show what was ratified then, to supply rationale, or to document a difference.
